analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate lower drug prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices was referred to the Finance Committee in April 2016 and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have removed the long-standing ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices. Instead, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would be required to negotiate lower prices for high-cost drugs — those with high per-beneficiary spending, high total program spending, large unit-cost increases, or high launch prices — and could negotiate for other drugs too. It would also require public reports on Part D drug spending. It was introduced by Senator Al Franken with two Democratic cosponsors and never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, including the roughly 40 million people in Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage, who would pay less out of pocket as negotiated discounts flowed into plan pricing. Taxpayers would also gain, since federal money covers a large share of Part D costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the Medicare 'noninterference' provision — the rule that barred the government from negotiating drug prices — and requires the Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with manufacturers for drugs deemed appropriate for negotiation. [S3]
Drugs are selected for required negotiation based on concrete cost factors: spending per beneficiary, total program spending, unit-cost increases over preceding years, and initial launch price. [S3]

The Secretary must report to Congress every six months on the negotiations, on Part D spending for the costliest drugs, and on drugs with no therapeutic substitutes, and must publish those reports on the CMS website. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose government-set negotiating baseline currently lets them charge Medicare plan sponsors uncontrolled prices. Lower negotiated prices would reduce their revenue on high-cost drugs.

drawbacks.text: The requirement is limited: the Secretary must negotiate only for drugs he or she deems 'appropriate' under the cost criteria, and merely 'may' negotiate for all other Part D drugs, so the scope of savings depends heavily on administrative choices. [S3]

Lower negotiated prices would reduce revenue for brand-name manufacturers, and an honest supporter would acknowledge the standard objection that reduced drug revenue could mean less investment in developing new medicines.
The bill requires negotiation but sets no enforcement mechanism or price target in the text, so it does not guarantee specific savings for beneficiaries. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: Medicare Part D is one of the biggest drug buyers in the world, and the bill targets exactly the drugs where spending and price increases are highest. The main cost falls on a single concentrated industry rather than being spread across the public. The design is modest rather than sweeping — negotiation is discretionary for most drugs and lacks enforcement teeth — but the core change, repealing the ban on negotiation, is direct and substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2016 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Al Franken introduced the Prescription Drug and Health Improvement Act of 2016 on April 27, 2016, for himself and Senator Amy Klobuchar. [S3]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced. [S5]
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still in committee. [S5]
The bill had two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support listed. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers benefited: the ban on Medicare price negotiation stayed in place and they continued selling to Part D plans at uncontrolled prices. Seniors and taxpayers got no relief.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral for all Medicare legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on April 27, 2016 and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry
against.what_they_did: Long opposed letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices and defended the existing 'noninterference' rule, which this bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor listed, and a Republican-controlled Senate never brought it to the floor.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 'noninterference' rule and requires the government to negotiate prices for high-cost drugs, directly cutting into manufacturer revenue on Medicare's biggest drug purchases. Lower negotiated prices would flow to seniors and taxpayers as lower premiums and federal costs. [S3]

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plans
industries.note: Negotiated government prices would be charged to Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations, changing how plans manage drug pricing, but the bill does not regulate them directly. [S3]
